questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1. It is split into 4 equal jumps. What fraction is one jump?
questions.explain: Count the equal spaces between the marks. There are 4 spaces, so each jump is 1/4. The common trap is counting the tick marks (5) instead of the spaces (4).

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1. It is split into 6 equal jumps. You start at 0 and make 3 jumps. What fraction are you at?
questions.explain: Each jump is 1/6, so 3 jumps put you at 3/6. You do not write just the number 3; you must include the denominator to show the size of each jump.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1. It is split into 5 equal jumps. You start at 0 and make 2 jumps. What fraction are you at?
questions.explain: Two jumps of 1/5 land you at 2/5. The denominator stays 5 because the line has 5 equal parts, not 6.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1. It is split into 8 equal jumps. What fraction is one jump?
questions.explain: There are 8 equal spaces, so one jump is 1/8. Counting the 9 tick marks would give the wrong denominator.

questions.question: For a board game, Leo draws a path from 0 to 1. He marks 5 equal jumps. His friend says, 'Jump 3 times from 0.' What fraction does Leo land on?
questions.explain: Three jumps of 1/5 put Leo at 3/5. He is not at the whole number 3; the line only goes from 0 to 1.

questions.question: A baker splits a 1-metre log cake into 4 equal slices for a party. She gives 1 slice to a child. What fraction of the whole cake is that slice?
questions.explain: One slice out of 4 equal slices is 1/4 of the cake. It is not the whole number 1, and there are 4 slices, not 5.

questions.question: For a science class, Aiden marks 1 metre of string with 6 equal jumps. He cuts at the 4th jump from 0. What fraction of the string is the cut piece?
questions.explain: The 4th jump of 1/6 is at 4/6 of the string. The denominator is 6 (the number of equal parts), not 7.

questions.question: For a math game, the number line goes from 0 to 1 with 10 equal jumps. You jump 7 times from 0. What fraction are you at?
questions.explain: Seven jumps of 1/10 put you at 7/10. You have 10 equal parts, not 11, so the denominator is 10.

questions.question: A number line from 0 to 1 is split into 6 equal jumps. You start at 0, jump 4 times, then jump back 1 time. What fraction are you at now?
questions.explain: 4 jumps forward minus 1 jump back is 3 jumps total, so you are at 3/6. Remember to subtract the jump back, and keep the denominator as 6.

questions.question: A number line from 0 to 1 is split into 4 equal jumps. A child says, 'After 3 jumps from 0, I am at 3.' What did the child get wrong?
options: The child counted 4 tick marks, not the spaces.
The child said a whole number, not a fraction.
The child made 4 jumps instead of just 3.
The child started counting at 1, not at 0.
questions.explain: After 3 jumps the child should say 3/4, a fraction. Saying just '3' treats the fraction like a whole number, which is the mistake here.

questions.question: A number line goes from 0 to 1 with 8 equal jumps. Ravi jumps 2 times from 0. Then he jumps 3 more times. What fraction is he on?
questions.explain: Count the spaces you jump, not the lines: 2 jumps and 3 more jumps is 5 spaces out of 8, so 5/8. Counting the lines gives 6/8, which is one space too far.

questions.question: Emma draws a number line from 0 to 1 on the board. She splits it into 4 equal jumps. Where does 3/4 go?
questions.explain: 3/4 means 3 equal spaces from 0, so jump 3 quarter jumps forward. The 3rd line counting 0 is only 2 spaces, which is 2/4.
